extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century English readers (churchgoers, coffee-house patrons, young women choosing husbands) / general readers interested in manners and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: A set of short prescriptive essays (Spectator-style) giving practical standards for public reading of prayers, coffee-house and conversational behaviour, dress, and choosing a husband; addressed to polite society. The page collects norms and examples for how to behave, speak, dress, and choose companions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper reading of the Common Prayer
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading the Common Prayer should be done with clearness, emphatic and fervent delivery so as to engage the congregation and make the worshipper address the Almighty rather than merely run the words as a form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read with clearness, loudness, and strength; adopt a decent behaviour and comely bodily posture (avoid folding arms and lolling on the book); speak deliberately (not too fast); aim for an evenness of voice and delivery; place the emphasis and give the proper accent to each word; vary the voice according to the nature of the sentence; conclude sentences with a gentle cadence; use an accent and turn peculiar to prayer rather than a familiar, gentleman-like tone; appoint exemplary readers (e.g. at Sion-College assemblies) to serve as patterns. Anti-patterns given: reading as if of 'a Gazette', 'pindarick' readers (uneven measure, alternating extreme slowness and speed), careless indifferency, and mend-the-language liberties (changing words like 'Pardoneth' to 'Pardons').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'cant' and inappropriate religious affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish cant (a whining, sudden-exclamatory, unskillful manner of prayer/preaching associated with low or rustic practice) from a proper elevation and emphasis in public prayer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake proper elevation of voice, due emphasis, and proper cadence for cant; cant is characterised by sudden jumps from low to high, whining tones, unusual exclamations, and misplaced emphasis (e.g., stressing insignificant particles like 'if' or 'and'). Proper skill in tone should be cultivated, not avoided for fear of seeming canting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplary readers to teach proper delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical remedy for poor reading habits is to provide a visible model: propose a person of great ability in reading to serve as a pattern at clergy assemblies and conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have an admired reader perform at public clerical gatherings (Sion-College and others) so that timid or affected readers can learn clear articulation, evenness, posture, deliberate pace, emphasis and appropriate variation of voice by example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public decorum in coffee-houses: avoid disruptive spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Coffee-house patrons should not perform disruptive musical or theatrical displays (singing volitionally, dancing, excessive coughing/spitting) that interrupt conversation and civility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of misconduct: singing a voluntary in spite of the company, dancing in the middle of the room, prolonged coughing and spitting to clear the throat, and treating the room as a stage. Proposed social sanctions: ostracism (declaring the offender an outlaw), penal social measures (refusing favors, limiting hospitality), and public reproof. The essay treats such behaviour as intolerable breaches of public manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be a pert, talkative impertinent in public
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid being the forward, talkative person who disregards the social observations of others and assumes all they say is of universal interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons appear foreign to English bashfulness and produce discomfort; they should be recognized as breaches of public decorum. The norm is modesty and awareness of others' attention and convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loud speakers and declaimers in mixed company
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from speaking so loud as to treat others as deaf or to dominate the room; loudness is often vanity or overvaluation of one's own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loud speakers persecute listeners and assume undue importance; the ideal conversationalist modulates voice to respect others' ears and the shared public space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be the whisperer who traffics in half-accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whisperers who pretend to secrets and tell half-stories (mixing whisper and loud asides) are socially offensive and rely on mechanical arts of seeming wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the affectation of secrecy used to enhance one's perceived importance; do not deal in half accounts or 'the town says' gossip. Genuine trustworthiness requires substance, not theatrical whispers; the whisperer's pattern of 'I will tell you a secret soon' is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing between suitors: abstract from circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding between two lovers differing mainly in fortune, imagine each in the other's circumstances; prefer the man whose behaviour is due to intrinsic quality rather than the opportunistic effects of wealth or poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Florio in Strephon's estate would still behave with the same modesty (or Strephon in Florio's condition would remain obsequious) choose the one whose personal qualities are stable across circumstances. Ask whether each values you for yourself or for fortune; prefer obliging (not merely receiving an obligation); prefer the man you would value for his own sake because his intrinsic qualities are more likely to produce stable happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a happy marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: A happy marriage arises where two persons voluntarily choose each other without principally regarding fortune or beauty, and where mutual affection and shared taste exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish marriage types: 'insipid' marriages (made solely by settlement and fortune, producing dull undistinguished lives), 'vexatious' marriages (two quick-tempered people matched to secure wealth, producing constant constraint and mutual reviling), and 'happy' marriages (voluntary choice, mutual esteem, ability to love through adversity). To choose well, consider who will like you undressed and tolerate your humours; prefer intrinsic over adventitious qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer intrinsic personal qualities to adventitious fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: If you must choose, employ fortune upon certainties rather than sacrificing certainties to fortune: prefer a partner whose personal perfections are reliable and improvable over one chosen for wealth alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A man taken for his personal perfections may, through marriage or otherwise, acquire fortune; a man taken for fortune will rarely gain intrinsic perfections through marriage. Practical maxim: 'employ Fortune upon Certainties, but do not sacrifice Certainties to Fortune.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress: avoid both the sloven and the fop; aim for tasteful establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothing should avoid deliberate slovenry (affecting rags or neglect) and ostentatious foppishness; the sensible course is a medium appropriate to one's station, preferably a habit rather above rather than below one's fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slovenry debases a person's standing and invites ridicule; a handsom suit of clothes procures respect (e.g., bankers bow more to well-dressed persons). Advice from Osbourn cited: appear rather above than below your fortune. Dressing beneath one's quality invites contempt and insults (example: an elderly man in threadbare dress insulted in a coffee-house). Avoid the vulgar custom of appearing sloven as a mark of wit; the medium between fop and sloven is the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against making pleasure the chief pursuit (man of wit and pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making pleasure the main purpose of life corrupts reason and reflection, leading to inconstancy, irresponsibility, damaged friendships, family ruin, and loss of enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs of the life devoted to pleasure: neglectful friendship, bad fatherhood, bankruptcies, mortgages, procrastination, dishonour, and a poverty of substantive pleasures despite constant indulgence. Pleasure addicts become unable to enjoy ordinary satisfactions, act impertinently or cruelly, and waste talents. The essay counsels against admiring those who sacrifice duty and steadiness for mere gaiety; the few brilliant geniuses who lived thus should not license the generality to mimic them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value in certain conversational qualities (example: military men)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain classes (here, military men) produce especially pleasant conversation because it is full of incidents, frankness, and magnanimity derived from their life and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for frank, incident-rich speech: soldiers' conversation is amiable and instructive because of their adventures and reflection. This functions as a positive norm for desirable conversational tone: candid, illustrative, and manly without frivolous affectation.
